Name: Anitta Text
Short Description: A royal narrative attributed to Anitta of Kanesh, recounting his conquests in central Anatolia and his father Pithana’s seizure of Kanesh. It records Anitta’s destruction and cursing of Hattusa, warning that any future ruler who rebuilt it would face divine punishment. Preserved in later Hittite copies, the text combines political memory, military achievement, and divine sanction to establish Anitta’s authority and dynastic legacy.

Name: Edict of Telipinu
Short Description: A royal proclamation combining a selective history of the early Hittite dynasty with rules for royal succession. Telipinu describes how murder, exile, and rivalry weakened the ruling house, then sets out an order of succession and limits punishment for political crimes to the offender rather than the wider family. The edict presents these reforms as a restoration of lawful and divinely favored order, while also strengthening Telipinu’s own legitimacy.

Name: Hittite Laws
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Dialectics (Conflict), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: A collection of nearly two hundred legal clauses preserved and revised from the Old Hittite period into the empire’s final centuries. Written largely in casuistic form (“If… then…”), the laws regulate injury, property, labor, family relations, sexual offenses, and ritual violations. Penalties vary according to status and circumstance, and later versions sometimes replace harsher punishments with compensation. The collection reflects royal efforts to order a stratified society through an evolving legal tradition and is among the earliest substantial legal corpora preserved in an Indo-European language.

Name: Purulli Festival Ritual
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: Festival texts associated with the Purulli spring celebration at Nerik, preserving an older Hattic cult tradition in Hittite form. Royal and priestly rites included offerings, invocations, and the recitation of the Storm God’s struggle with Illuyanka. The festival sought divine protection, agricultural prosperity, and the proper renewal of the land. By integrating a regional spring rite into the state cult, it may also have reinforced the sacred responsibilities and legitimacy of Hittite kingship.

Name: The Song of Kumarbi
Short Description: A Hittite version of a Hurrian divine-succession tradition, also known as the Song of Going Forth. It recounts the transfer of heavenly kingship from Alalu to Anu and then to Kumarbi, who attacks Anu and becomes pregnant with several gods, including the Storm God Teshub. Fragmentary and symbolically dense, the poem combines cosmic violence, bodily generation, and rivalry among divine generations. It can be read as an exploration of how sovereignty is seized, inherited, and repeatedly contested, and it provided a major regional model for later succession myths.

Name: Treaty of Kadesh
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Dialectics (Conflict), Subversion (Negation), Becoming (Process Ontology)
Short Description: A peace and alliance treaty concluded between Ramesses II of Egypt and Ḫattušili III of Hatti after years of rivalry between the two powers. It establishes non-aggression, mutual defense, succession support, and the return of fugitives. Preserved in Akkadian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphic versions, it is the earliest surviving peace treaty for which texts from both parties are known. The versions frame the agreement somewhat differently, with the Egyptian presentation favoring Ramesses, while both invoke divine witnesses and curses to sacralize the settlement.

Name: Apology of Hattusili III
Short Description: A first-person royal account in which Hattusili III defends his seizure of the throne from his nephew Urhi-Teshub. He recounts his sickly childhood, the protection of the goddess Šauška of Samuha, and his rise through military and political office. The text presents his overthrow of Urhi-Teshub as divinely favored and politically necessary rather than a criminal usurpation. Serving as both autobiography and royal propaganda, it shows how personal history, theology, and bureaucratic recordkeeping could be used to legitimize contested kingship.

Name: The Myth of Illuyanka
Metaphysical Tags: Dialectics (Conflict), Subversion (Negation), Becoming (Process Ontology), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: Two related versions recount the Storm God’s defeat by the serpent Illuyanka and his eventual recovery. In one, the goddess Inara and the mortal Hupasiya lure the serpent and its family to a feast, allowing the Storm God to strike. In the other, the Storm God fathers a son who marries Illuyanka’s daughter and retrieves his father’s stolen heart and eyes; the son then dies alongside the serpent in the final battle. Embedded in the Purulli festival tradition, the myth links divine recovery and victory with renewed order, protection, and prosperity.

Name: Instructions to Priests and Temple Officials
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Dialectics (Conflict), Phenomenology (Experiential)
Short Description: A set of royal instructions regulating the conduct of priests and temple personnel, including ritual timing, purity, food handling, safeguarding offerings, and the proper use of divine property. Negligence and corruption are threatened with both royal and divine punishment. The text treats cult service as disciplined administrative labor and links failures in temple management to danger for the gods, the king, and the land. It therefore shows how religious practice and bureaucratic supervision could support the stability of the Hittite state.

Name: The Song of Ullikummi
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Dialectics (Conflict), Clockwork (Causal Determinism)
Short Description: Part of the Hurrian-Hittite Kumarbi Cycle, the poem tells how Kumarbi produces the stone giant Ullikummi and places him on the shoulders of the primordial being Upelluri to challenge the Storm God Teshub. Ullikummi grows toward heaven and overwhelms the gods until Ea retrieves the ancient cutting tool once used to separate heaven and earth and severs the giant from his foundation. Preserved in Hittite and Hurrian fragments, the narrative dramatizes a radical challenge to established divine sovereignty. Its opposition between disruptive force and restored order may have resonated with political anxieties about rebellion and imperial continuity, though it does not describe any identifiable historical uprising.
